Chapter 8: Nature and Technology—Finding Balance in a Digital Age.
You know, these days, technology is just part of life. It’s everywhere—woven right into our routines, our families, our moments together. But here’s the real challenge: how do we welcome all the good things screens can offer, without losing our sense of connection to the world outside?
Picture this—a teenager sitting at her desk, scrolling through social media. She’s chatting with friends from all over the world, but underneath it all, she feels a little restless, maybe even distracted. Her mom suggests taking a walk in the park. At first, the idea doesn’t sound too appealing, but eventually, the girl gives in—and of course, she brings her phone.
As they wander, she starts snapping photos of wildflowers and posting them online. Suddenly, her friends are asking questions about the plants, the park, wanting to know more. In that moment, something clicks—the digital and natural worlds aren’t so separate after all. They can actually enrich each other.
It turns out, when we use tech with intention, it can bring us even closer to nature. There are apps that help you identify birds or trees, track your hikes, or share your discoveries. Online groups can organize park clean-ups, group hikes, or even citizen science projects. Maybe you know some kids who, after watching a nature documentary, start a blog to share their adventures in a local wetland. Before long, they’ve drawn in classmates, neighbors—maybe even you.
But let’s be honest—there’s a flip side. Screens can easily take over, pulling our attention away from the gentle rustle of leaves, the shimmer of sunlight on water, or the feeling of wind on our skin. It’s easy to just turn to digital entertainment, and miss out on those small, magical moments that nature offers.
So what’s the answer? It all comes down to being intentional. Set aside some “tech-free” hours—turn off the devices, and just step outside. Let yourself be bored, let your mind wander, and see what you notice.
Lots of families are trying this out. Some schedule unplugged time together, while schools might offer outdoor learning days, teaching lessons under the open sky. Even at work, people are starting to take walking meetings, or eat lunch in a nearby park.
And here’s what most of us find: it’s not about strict rules or cutting out technology altogether. It’s about being aware—learning to notice when your devices help you connect, and when they pull you away. The real goal isn’t to escape the digital world, but to use it as a bridge, a way to invite the wild back into your everyday life.
